blocks.en: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us … full of grace and truth."
blocks.es_reference: «Y aquel Verbo fue hecho carne, y habitó entre nosotros … lleno de gracia y de verdad».

blocks.en: Unit Scripture: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." — John 1:14 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Escritura de la Unidad: «Y aquel Verbo fue hecho carne, y habitó entre nosotros, y vimos su gloria, gloria como del unigénito del Padre, lleno de gracia y de verdad». — Juan 1:14 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation: The Word Behind the Word
blocks.es_reference: Orientación: La palabra detrás de la palabra

blocks.en: Open a King James Bible to 1 Corinthians 13 and read the famous closing verse: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Most modern readers stumble at that word. Charity? In English today, "charity" means donations to the poor, or a tax-deductible non-profit organization. It is a thin, financial word. We expect this verse to say "love," and indeed every modern translation does. So why "charity" in the KJV?
blocks.es_reference: Abre una Biblia King James en inglés en 1 Corintios 13 y lee el famoso versículo final: «Y ahora permanecen fe, esperanza, charity, estas tres; pero la mayor de ellas es charity». La mayoría de los lectores modernos tropieza con esa palabra. ¿Charity? En inglés hoy, charity significa donaciones a los pobres, o una organización sin fines de lucro deducible de impuestos. Es una palabra delgada y financiera. Esperamos que este versículo diga «amor», y de hecho toda traducción moderna así lo hace. ¿Por qué entonces «charity» en la KJV?

blocks.en: Because behind the English word stands a Greek word the King James translators in 1611 chose to render through its Latin form. The Greek is agapê (αγαπη). When Jerome translated the New Testament into Latin around AD 400, he rendered agapê as caritas. Centuries later, caritas came into English as charity. Then, slowly, the English word narrowed and shrank. By 1611 the KJV translators still felt the old fullness in "charity." By 2025 the word means almost nothing of what Paul meant. Every translator faces this dilemma: the Greek word holds more than any one English word can carry. Translation always loses something. The only way to recover what is lost is to learn the Greek word itself.
blocks.es_reference: Porque detrás de la palabra inglesa está una palabra griega que los traductores de la King James en 1611 eligieron traducir por su forma latina. El griego es agapê (αγαπη). Cuando Jerónimo tradujo el Nuevo Testamento al latín alrededor del año 400 d.C., tradujo agapê como caritas. Siglos después, caritas entró al inglés como charity. Luego, lentamente, la palabra inglesa se estrechó y encogió. Para 1611 los traductores de la KJV todavía sentían la antigua plenitud en «charity». Para 2025 la palabra significa casi nada de lo que Pablo quiso decir. Todo traductor enfrenta este dilema: la palabra griega contiene más de lo que cualquier palabra inglesa o española puede cargar. La traducción siempre pierde algo. La única manera de recuperar lo perdido es aprender la palabra griega misma.

blocks.en: "Charity" in 1611 was the full Greek agapê. By today the English word has shrunk to a tax-deduction. The Greek did not change. Our English did.
blocks.es_reference: «Charity» en 1611 era la plenitud griega de agapê. Hoy la palabra inglesa se ha encogido a una deducción de impuestos. El griego no cambió. Nuestra traducción sí.

blocks.en: Why this unit matters
blocks.es_reference: Por qué importa esta unidad

blocks.en: The first seven units of Language Appreciation built the foundation: the textual story (Units 1–2), the Hebrew alphabet (Units 3–4), the Hebrew word treasures (Unit 5), and the Greek alphabet (Units 6–7). You can now read Greek and Hebrew letters. Unit 8 is where the work begins to pay back. Today we open four Greek words — just four — and the New Testament will look different forever. We will not learn grammar tonight. We will not parse verbs. We will simply lift the lid off four boxes the English Bible packs flat for transport: Logos, Agapê, Charis, Pneuma. Word, love, grace, spirit. Open each one and there is more inside than the English carton can hold.
blocks.es_reference: Las primeras siete unidades de Apreciación de Lenguas Bíblicas construyeron el fundamento: la historia textual (Unidades 1–2), el alfabeto hebreo (Unidades 3–4), los tesoros de palabras hebreas (Unidad 5), y el alfabeto griego (Unidades 6–7). Ya puedes leer letras griegas y hebreas. La Unidad 8 es donde el trabajo empieza a dar fruto. Hoy abrimos cuatro palabras griegas — solo cuatro — y el Nuevo Testamento se verá diferente para siempre. No aprenderemos gramática esta noche. No analizaremos verbos. Simplemente levantaremos la tapa de cuatro cajas que la Biblia castellana empaca planas para el transporte: Logos, Agapê, Charis, Pneuma. Verbo, amor, gracia, espíritu. Abre cada una y hay más dentro de lo que el cartón castellano puede contener.

blocks.en: Notice the providence of our unit scripture. John 1:14 contains two of these four words. "And the Word (Logos) became flesh and dwelt among us … full of grace (charis) and truth." John could not have introduced the Incarnation any more economically. Unit 9 will pick up four more great Greek words (faith, save, righteousness, Lord). Then Unit 10 puts Strong's numbers in your hand and Unit 11 is your first real word study. You are climbing the last hill of the course.
blocks.es_reference: Nota la providencia de nuestra escritura. Juan 1:14 contiene dos de estas cuatro palabras. «Y aquel Verbo (Logos) fue hecho carne, y habitó entre nosotros … lleno de gracia (charis) y de verdad». Juan no podría haber introducido la Encarnación con mayor economía. La Unidad 9 retomará cuatro grandes palabras griegas más (fe, salvar, justicia, Señor). Luego la Unidad 10 te pone los números de Strong en la mano y la Unidad 11 es tu primer estudio real de palabras. Estás subiendo la última cuesta del curso.

blocks.en: I. LOGOS (λόγος) — The Word Who Is a Person
blocks.es_reference: I. LOGOS (λόγος) — La Palabra que es una Persona

blocks.en: word, speech, reason, account, principle, the divine self-expression made Person in Christ
blocks.es_reference: palabra, discurso, razón, cuenta, principio, la auto-expresión divina hecha Persona en Cristo

blocks.en: Five hundred years before Christ, a melancholy Greek philosopher named Heraclitus stood by a river in Ephesus and announced that you cannot step in the same river twice. Everything flows. Everything changes. But beneath all the flux, Heraclitus said, there is one steady reality holding the universe together: the logos. The cosmic Reason. The Principle behind everything. To Heraclitus the logos was an idea, an impersonal structure, the deep order of the cosmos.
blocks.es_reference: Quinientos años antes de Cristo, un filósofo griego melancólico llamado Heráclito estaba parado junto a un río en Éfeso y anunció que no puedes pisar el mismo río dos veces. Todo fluye. Todo cambia. Pero debajo de todo el flujo, dijo Heráclito, hay una realidad firme que sostiene unido al universo: el logos. La Razón cósmica. El Principio detrás de todo. Para Heráclito el logos era una idea, una estructura impersonal, el orden profundo del cosmos.

blocks.en: For five centuries Greek philosophers refined this notion. The Stoics built whole systems on the logos. Educated Greeks of the first century did not need the word explained — "logos" was as familiar to them as "evolution" or "energy" is to us today. And then, around AD 85–95, an old fisherman from Galilee picked up his pen at Ephesus and opened his Gospel with seventeen words that detonated the entire philosophical tradition. "En archê ên ho Logos." In the beginning was the Logos.
blocks.es_reference: Durante cinco siglos los filósofos griegos refinaron esta noción. Los estoicos construyeron sistemas enteros sobre el logos. Los griegos educados del siglo primero no necesitaban que les explicaran la palabra — «logos» les era tan familiar como «evolución» o «energía» lo es para nosotros hoy. Y entonces, alrededor de los años 85–95 d.C., un viejo pescador de Galilea tomó su pluma en Éfeso y abrió su Evangelio con diecisiete palabras que detonaron toda la tradición filosófica. «En archê ên ho Logos». En el principio era el Logos.

blocks.en: Every educated Greek who read that opening sentence sat forward in his chair. The logos? The cosmic principle? In the beginning? Yes — and now John drops the hammer. "And the Logos was with God, and the Logos was God." The logos is not a principle. The logos is a Person. And then, in verse 14, the line that no Greek philosopher had ever even imagined was possible: "And the Logos became flesh and dwelt among us." The abstract universal Principle did not stay abstract. He became a baby in a manger, a boy in Nazareth, a carpenter in a shop, a Rabbi by the lake, a Sacrifice on a cross. The cosmic Logos has a face. His name is Jesus.
blocks.es_reference: Todo griego educado que leyó esa oración inicial se enderezó en su silla. ¿El logos? ¿El principio cósmico? ¿En el principio? Sí — y ahora Juan deja caer el martillo. «Y el Logos era con Dios, y el Logos era Dios». El logos no es un principio. El logos es una Persona. Y luego, en el versículo 14, la línea que ningún filósofo griego había siquiera imaginado posible: «Y aquel Logos fue hecho carne, y habitó entre nosotros». El Principio universal abstracto no permaneció abstracto. Se hizo bebé en un pesebre, niño en Nazaret, carpintero en un taller, Rabí junto al lago, Sacrificio en una cruz. El Logos cósmico tiene un rostro. Su nombre es Jesús.

blocks.en: You can read John 1:1 a hundred times in English. But the moment you read it once in Greek — En archê ên ho Logos — the verse acquires a depth no translation can deliver. The Logos is the divine self-expression of God Almighty, and He stepped out of eternity into a teenage girl's womb in Bethlehem. That is the Christmas story in one Greek word.
blocks.es_reference: Puedes leer Juan 1:1 cien veces en español. Pero el momento que lo lees una vez en griego — En archê ên ho Logos — el versículo adquiere una profundidad que ninguna traducción puede entregar. El Logos es la auto-expresión divina de Dios Todopoderoso, y dio un paso fuera de la eternidad hacia el vientre de una joven en Belén. Esa es la historia de Navidad en una palabra griega.

blocks.en: How this changes Bible reading
blocks.es_reference: Cómo esto cambia la lectura bíblica

blocks.en: When the Gospel of John speaks of the Word, this is not a synonym for "Bible verse" or "spoken sentence." It is a title for Christ — the eternal, pre-existent Second Person of the Trinity. When John 1:14 says the Word "became flesh," the Greek verb is egeneto, "became" — not "appeared as," not "looked like," not "seemed to be." The Eternal Logos truly took on human flesh. Christmas is not God dressing up as a man. Christmas is God becoming a man without ceasing to be God. The Greek word logos guards this doctrine. Every cult that denies the deity of Christ has to wrestle with John 1:1 in Greek and lose.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando el Evangelio de Juan habla del Verbo, esto no es sinónimo de «versículo bíblico» u «oración hablada». Es un título para Cristo — la eterna, preexistente Segunda Persona de la Trinidad. Cuando Juan 1:14 dice que el Verbo «fue hecho carne», el verbo griego es egeneto, «vino a ser» — no «apareció como», no «parecía», no «daba la impresión de ser». El Logos Eterno verdaderamente tomó sobre sí carne humana. La Navidad no es Dios disfrazándose de hombre. La Navidad es Dios haciéndose hombre sin dejar de ser Dios. La palabra griega logos guarda esta doctrina. Toda secta que niega la deidad de Cristo tiene que luchar con Juan 1:1 en griego y perder.

blocks.en: II. AGAPÊ (ἀγάπη) — The Love That Has No Other Name
blocks.es_reference: II. AGAPÊ (ἀγάπη) — El amor que no tiene otro nombre

blocks.en: self-giving, sacrificial, unconditional love — the love God is
blocks.es_reference: amor abnegado, sacrificial, incondicional — el amor que Dios es

blocks.en: Greek has four words where English has one. C.S. Lewis wrote a small book in 1960 called The Four Loves that opens this drawer for the English reader. Each of the four Greek words names a different kind of love, and learning the four sharpens every "love your neighbor" passage in the New Testament.
blocks.es_reference: El griego tiene cuatro palabras donde el español tiene una. C.S. Lewis escribió un pequeño libro en 1960 llamado Los Cuatro Amores que abre este cajón para el lector castellano. Cada una de las cuatro palabras griegas nombra un tipo diferente de amor, y aprender las cuatro afila cada pasaje de «amar al prójimo» en el Nuevo Testamento.

blocks.en: <th>Greek</th><th>Transliteration</th><th>Kind of love</th><th>Example</th>
blocks.es_reference: <th>Griego</th><th>Transliteración</th><th>Tipo de amor</th><th>Ejemplo</th>

blocks.en: ἜρωςerosRomantic, passionate desireHusband and wife (Song of Solomon)
blocks.es_reference: ἜρωςerosDeseo romántico y apasionadoEsposo y esposa (Cantar de los Cantares)

blocks.en: ΦιλίαphiliaFriendship between equalsDavid and Jonathan
blocks.es_reference: ΦιλίαphiliaAmistad entre igualesDavid y Jonatán

blocks.en: ΣτοργήstorgêFamily affection — parent and childMary holding the infant Jesus
blocks.es_reference: ΣτοργήstorgêAfecto familiar — padre e hijoMaría sosteniendo al niño Jesús

blocks.en: ἈγάπηagapêSelf-giving love regardless of returnChrist on the cross for sinners
blocks.es_reference: ἈγάπηagapêAmor abnegado sin importar la respuestaCristo en la cruz por los pecadores

blocks.en: Here is the surprise. In classical pre-Christian Greek, agapê was the weakest and rarest of the four. Eros was strong — passionate, urgent, sometimes destructive. Philia was strong — the love Aristotle wrote whole books about. Storgê was strong — the bond of mother and child. Agapê, by comparison, was a pale, generic, almost colorless word for "fondness" or "esteem." When the New Testament authors needed a word for divine love, they could have grabbed any of the four. They chose the weakest. They chose the empty cup. Then they filled it.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí está la sorpresa. En el griego clásico precristiano, agapê era la más débil y rara de las cuatro. Eros era fuerte — apasionado, urgente, a veces destructivo. Philia era fuerte — el amor sobre el cual Aristóteles escribió libros enteros. Storgê era fuerte — el vínculo de madre e hijo. Agapê, en comparación, era una palabra pálida, genérica, casi incolora para «cariño» o «estima». Cuando los autores del Nuevo Testamento necesitaron una palabra para el amor divino, podrían haber tomado cualquiera de las cuatro. Eligieron la más débil. Eligieron la copa vacía. Luego la llenaron.

blocks.en: Why? Because the strong words were contaminated. Eros carried sexual desire. Philia required mutual liking. Storgê required blood relation. None of those words could carry the new freight: a love that crosses every tribe, gives without return, and seeks the good of an enemy. They needed a clean word. Agapê was the closest empty container Greek had. So Paul, John, Peter, and the others poured the very nature of God into it. By the time the New Testament was finished, agapê had become the highest word in the Greek language. The empty cup now overflowed.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Por qué? Porque las palabras fuertes estaban contaminadas. Eros cargaba deseo sexual. Philia requería simpatía mutua. Storgê requería relación de sangre. Ninguna de esas palabras podía cargar la nueva carga: un amor que cruza toda tribu, da sin retorno, y busca el bien de un enemigo. Necesitaban una palabra limpia. Agapê era el contenedor vacío más cercano que tenía el griego. Así que Pablo, Juan, Pedro, y los demás vertieron la naturaleza misma de Dios en ella. Para cuando el Nuevo Testamento se terminó, agapê se había convertido en la palabra más alta del idioma griego. La copa vacía ahora rebosaba.

blocks.en: The Greeks gave us the empty cup. The Holy Spirit filled it with the love of God. That is agapê.
blocks.es_reference: Los griegos nos dieron la copa vacía. El Espíritu Santo la llenó con el amor de Dios. Eso es agapê.

blocks.en: 1 John 4:8 in Greek
blocks.es_reference: 1 Juan 4:8 en griego

blocks.en: The shortest theological sentence in the Greek New Testament is four words: ho theos agapê estin. "God is love." Notice: God does not merely have love. God is love. Agapê is not a feeling God has when He is in a good mood. Agapê is the eternal essence of His being. Before the foundation of the world — before there was anyone to love — the three Persons of the Trinity were already pouring agapê into one another in perfect, unbroken fellowship. The God who is agapê created you because He wanted to share that fellowship outward. That is the Christian doctrine of creation, in one Greek noun.
blocks.es_reference: La oración teológica más corta en el Nuevo Testamento griego es de cuatro palabras: ho theos agapê estin. «Dios es amor». Nota: Dios no meramente tiene amor. Dios es amor. Agapê no es un sentimiento que Dios tiene cuando está de buen humor. Agapê es la esencia eterna de Su ser. Antes de la fundación del mundo — antes de que hubiera alguien a quien amar — las tres Personas de la Trinidad ya estaban derramando agapê unas en otras en comunión perfecta e ininterrumpida. El Dios que es agapê te creó porque quería compartir esa comunión hacia afuera. Esa es la doctrina cristiana de la creación, en un sustantivo griego.

blocks.en: The application
blocks.es_reference: La aplicación

blocks.en: Every time the New Testament commands you to "love" your neighbor, your enemy, your spouse, your brother, the word is almost always agapê. It is a command you can obey when you do not feel like it — because agapê is not a feeling. It is a decision of the will to seek another's good, regardless of how you feel about them. You cannot command eros; you cannot command storgê; you cannot really command philia. But agapê is exactly the love that can be commanded, because it does not depend on the worthiness of its object. That is why Jesus could command us to love our enemies. He used the only word that made the command possible.
blocks.es_reference: Cada vez que el Nuevo Testamento manda «amar» a tu prójimo, a tu enemigo, a tu cónyuge, a tu hermano, la palabra es casi siempre agapê. Es un mandato que puedes obedecer cuando no tienes ganas — porque agapê no es un sentimiento. Es una decisión de la voluntad de buscar el bien del otro, sin importar lo que sientas hacia él. No puedes mandar eros; no puedes mandar storgê; no puedes realmente mandar philia. Pero agapê es exactamente el amor que sí puede ser mandado, porque no depende del mérito de su objeto. Por eso Jesús pudo mandarnos amar a nuestros enemigos. Usó la única palabra que hacía posible el mandato.

blocks.en: III. CHARIS (χάρις) — The Gift That Cannot Be Repaid
blocks.es_reference: III. CHARIS (χάρις) — El regalo que no se puede pagar

blocks.en: grace, free favor, unearned gift, kindness without obligation
blocks.es_reference: gracia, favor inmerecido, regalo gratuito, bondad sin obligación

blocks.en: Greek charis shows up everywhere in English. The English family is enormous: charity (a related word, through Latin); charisma (a spiritual gift from God); charismatic; Eucharist (literally eu-charis-tia, "good-grace," our word for thanksgiving and the Lord's Supper); even grateful and gratis through the parallel Latin gratia. When you hear any English word with the "char" or "grat" root, the Greek charis stands behind it.
blocks.es_reference: El griego charis aparece por todas partes en el español. La familia es enorme: caridad (palabra relacionada, a través del latín); carisma (un don espiritual de Dios); carismático; Eucaristía (literalmente eu-charis-tia, «buena-gracia», nuestra palabra para la acción de gracias y la Cena del Señor); incluso grato y gratis a través del paralelo latino gratia. Cuando escuchas cualquier palabra castellana con la raíz «car» o «grat», el griego charis está detrás.

blocks.en: But here is the surprise. In classical pre-Christian Greek, charis did not mean "free gift." It meant exactly the opposite. Charis in ancient Athens was a favor done that placed the receiver under obligation to repay. It was the lubricant of the Mediterranean honor culture. A wealthy patron showed charis to a poor client — and the client owed him for life. Receiving charis was receiving a debt. You took the favor, you bowed, and you spent your future repaying. This is the world the early Christians grew up in.
blocks.es_reference: Pero aquí está la sorpresa. En el griego clásico precristiano, charis no significaba «regalo gratuito». Significaba exactamente lo contrario. Charis en la antigua Atenas era un favor hecho que ponía al receptor bajo obligación de pagarlo. Era el lubricante de la cultura mediterránea del honor. Un patrón rico mostraba charis a un cliente pobre — y el cliente le debía de por vida. Recibir charis era recibir una deuda. Tomabas el favor, te inclinabas, y gastabas tu futuro pagándolo. Este es el mundo en que crecieron los primeros cristianos.

blocks.en: Then Paul picks up the word and turns it inside-out. Ephesians 2:8–9: "By grace (chariti) are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast." Notice what Paul does. Charis, the Greek word that always created obligation, now creates the opposite of obligation. It creates a gift with no strings, no repayment plan, no honor-debt. God's charis is not a patron's favor that you spend your life paying off. It is the absolute opposite — the kind of gift you could not repay if you tried, the kind that is so completely free that boasting is excluded by definition. The pagan reader of Ephesians 2 in AD 60 would have stared at the page. This is not how charis works. Paul: For the Christian, this is now exactly how charis works.
blocks.es_reference: Entonces Pablo toma la palabra y le da la vuelta. Efesios 2:8–9: «Por gracia (chariti) sois salvos por medio de la fe; y esto no de vosotros, pues es don de Dios; no por obras, para que nadie se gloríe». Nota lo que hace Pablo. Charis, la palabra griega que siempre creaba obligación, ahora crea lo opuesto de la obligación. Crea un regalo sin condiciones, sin plan de pago, sin deuda de honor. La charis de Dios no es el favor de un patrón que gastas tu vida pagando. Es lo absolutamente opuesto — el tipo de regalo que no podrías pagar aunque lo intentaras, el tipo que es tan completamente gratuito que la gloria propia está excluida por definición. El lector pagano de Efesios 2 en el año 60 d.C. se habría quedado mirando la página. Así no funciona charis. Pablo: Para el cristiano, así es exactamente como charis funciona ahora.

blocks.en: In Athens, charis built an honor-debt. In Christ, charis destroys the honor-debt forever. That is why Paul says "not of works, lest any man should boast." Boasting is impossible in front of a gift that big.
blocks.es_reference: En Atenas, charis construía una deuda de honor. En Cristo, charis destruye la deuda de honor para siempre. Por eso Pablo dice «no por obras, para que nadie se gloríe». La gloria propia es imposible frente a un regalo tan grande.

blocks.en: John Newton and Amazing Grace
blocks.es_reference: John Newton y Sublime Gracia

blocks.en: If the doctrine sounds abstract, listen to a man who lived it. John Newton was born in London in 1725. By his twenties he was captain of a slave ship out of Liverpool, dealing in human beings, blaspheming Christ, and ruining his own soul. On March 21, 1748, his ship caught a storm so violent off the coast of Ireland that Newton expected to drown that night. In terror he cried out to a God he had spent years mocking. The ship survived. So did Newton's soul. He left the slave trade, studied for the ministry, became an Anglican parson at Olney in 1764, and in 1772 wrote a hymn for his New Year's Day sermon. The first line is six English words: "Amazing grace, how sweet the sound." The Greek word behind "grace" is charis. The man who wrote the song had once trafficked in human flesh. He had received a gift he could never repay, and he spent the rest of his life telling people about it. His tombstone in Olney churchyard, written by his own hand, says: "John Newton, Clerk, once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long laboured to destroy."
blocks.es_reference: Si la doctrina suena abstracta, escucha a un hombre que la vivió. John Newton nació en Londres en 1725. Para sus veintitantos años era capitán de un barco esclavista de Liverpool, traficando con seres humanos, blasfemando contra Cristo, y arruinando su propia alma. El 21 de marzo de 1748, su barco enfrentó una tormenta tan violenta frente a la costa de Irlanda que Newton esperaba ahogarse esa noche. Aterrorizado clamó a un Dios al que había pasado años burlándose. El barco sobrevivió. Y también el alma de Newton. Dejó el comercio de esclavos, estudió para el ministerio, se hizo clérigo anglicano en Olney en 1764, y en 1772 escribió un himno para su sermón de Año Nuevo. La primera línea en inglés es seis palabras: «Amazing grace, how sweet the sound» — «Sublime gracia, qué dulce el son». La palabra griega detrás de «gracia» es charis. El hombre que escribió la canción había una vez traficado con carne humana. Había recibido un regalo que nunca podría pagar, y pasó el resto de su vida contándolo a la gente. Su lápida en el cementerio de Olney, escrita por su propia mano, dice: «John Newton, Clérigo, una vez infiel y libertino, siervo de esclavos en África, fue, por la rica misericordia de nuestro Señor y Salvador Jesucristo, preservado, restaurado, perdonado, y nombrado para predicar la fe que tanto se había esforzado en destruir».

blocks.en: How this changes Bible reading
blocks.es_reference: Cómo esto cambia la lectura bíblica

blocks.en: Every time the New Testament says "grace," remember: this is not "the favor of a kindly God who likes nice people." This is the absolute, unrepayable, no-strings, boasting-excluded gift of God to undeserving sinners. Every time you read "Grace and peace from God our Father" at the start of a Paul letter, that is charis kai eirênê. Grace first, then peace. Without charis there is no peace. With charis, the peace is guaranteed because the gift cannot be revoked.
blocks.es_reference: Cada vez que el Nuevo Testamento dice «gracia», recuerda: esto no es «el favor de un Dios bondadoso que aprecia a la gente buena». Este es el regalo absoluto, impagable, sin condiciones, con la gloria propia excluida, de Dios para pecadores indignos. Cada vez que lees «Gracia y paz de Dios nuestro Padre» al principio de una carta de Pablo, eso es charis kai eirênê. Gracia primero, luego paz. Sin charis no hay paz. Con charis, la paz está garantizada porque el regalo no puede ser revocado.

blocks.en: IV. PNEUMA (πνεῦμα) — The Wind, The Breath, The Spirit
blocks.es_reference: IV. PNEUMA (πνεῦμα) — El viento, el aliento, el Espíritu

blocks.en: spirit, wind, breath — one Greek word for all three
blocks.es_reference: espíritu, viento, aliento — una sola palabra griega para los tres

blocks.en: The Greek word pneuma carries three meanings at once: wind, breath, and spirit. English has three separate words for these three ideas. Greek has one word that holds all three together. The Hebrew Old Testament had the very same arrangement with the word ruach (which we met in the Hebrew word treasures unit). What Hebrew did for the Old Testament, Greek does for the New. The invisible moving thing that makes branches sway and lungs fill and souls live is one reality to the biblical mind, and Scripture refuses to pull the three meanings apart.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra griega pneuma carga tres significados a la vez: viento, aliento, y espíritu. El español tiene tres palabras separadas para estas tres ideas. El griego tiene una palabra que mantiene los tres juntos. El Antiguo Testamento hebreo tenía exactamente el mismo arreglo con la palabra ruach (que conocimos en la unidad de tesoros de palabras hebreas). Lo que el hebreo hizo por el Antiguo Testamento, el griego lo hace por el Nuevo. La cosa invisible y en movimiento que hace que las ramas se mezan y que los pulmones se llenen y que las almas vivan es una sola realidad para la mente bíblica, y la Escritura se niega a separar los tres significados.

blocks.en: You already know pneuma through its English derivatives. Pneumonia is a disease of the lungs — the organ where breath happens. Pneumatic tools run on compressed air. A pneumatic tire is air-filled. The English word spirit goes back through Latin spiritus ("breath"), preserving the same insight: spirit is breath you cannot see. The Greek pneuma is the same insight at the source.
blocks.es_reference: Ya conoces pneuma a través de sus derivados en español. Pulmonía (en inglés pneumonia) es una enfermedad de los pulmones — el órgano donde sucede la respiración. Las herramientas neumáticas funcionan con aire comprimido. Una llanta neumática está llena de aire. La palabra espíritu viene del latín spiritus («aliento»), preservando la misma intuición: el espíritu es aliento que no se puede ver. El griego pneuma es la misma intuición en la fuente.

blocks.en: The Nicodemus dialogue (John 3)
blocks.es_reference: El diálogo con Nicodemo (Juan 3)

blocks.en: Now read John 3:8 in the King James and watch what Jesus does. "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit." Two different English words there — wind and Spirit. But in Greek, Jesus uses the same word twice: to pneuma hopou thelei pnei … houtôs estin pas ho gegennêmenos ek tou pneumatos. Literally: "The pneuma blows where it wills … so is everyone born of the pneuma." Nicodemus is hearing a pun the English-language reader misses every time. Jesus is saying: you cannot see this thing, but you can see what it does. The leaves move — you know there is wind. The sinner is reborn — you know there is Spirit. Same invisible Reality, two domains. The Greek wordplay is the whole point of the verse, and the English forces a choice between two words that the Greek deliberately holds together.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora lee Juan 3:8 en la Reina-Valera Gómez y observa lo que hace Jesús. «El viento de donde quiere sopla, y oyes su sonido; mas ni sabes de dónde viene, ni a dónde va; así es todo aquel que es nacido del Espíritu». Dos palabras castellanas diferentes — viento y Espíritu. Pero en griego, Jesús usa la misma palabra dos veces: to pneuma hopou thelei pnei … houtôs estin pas ho gegennêmenos ek tou pneumatos. Literalmente: «El pneuma sopla donde quiere … así es todo aquel nacido del pneuma». Nicodemo está escuchando un juego de palabras que el lector castellano se pierde cada vez. Jesús está diciendo: no puedes ver esto, pero puedes ver lo que hace. Las hojas se mueven — sabes que hay viento. El pecador renace — sabes que hay Espíritu. La misma Realidad invisible, dos dominios. El juego de palabras griego es todo el punto del versículo, y el castellano obliga a elegir entre dos palabras que el griego deliberadamente mantiene juntas.

blocks.en: Pneuma is one word for three things you cannot see: the wind in the trees, the breath in your lungs, the Spirit in the soul. Same God, three windows.
blocks.es_reference: Pneuma es una palabra para tres cosas que no se pueden ver: el viento en los árboles, el aliento en los pulmones, el Espíritu en el alma. Un mismo Dios, tres ventanas.

blocks.en: Acts 2 and Pentecost
blocks.es_reference: Hechos 2 y Pentecostés

blocks.en: On the morning of Pentecost, fifty days after the Resurrection, the disciples were gathered in an upper room. Acts 2:2: "And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting." The Greek word for "wind" here is actually pnoê, a close cousin of pneuma (same root, different ending). Two verses later the Holy Pneuma fills the disciples. Acts 2 deliberately runs the wind-and-Spirit wordplay across a single paragraph. The disciples first hear the wind, then they receive the Spirit, and they speak in tongues so that visitors from sixteen nations each hear the gospel in their own native language. The first sound of the church age was the sound of pneuma. The first miracle of the church age was language. (You are studying the right course.)
blocks.es_reference: En la mañana de Pentecostés, cincuenta días después de la Resurrección, los discípulos estaban reunidos en un aposento alto. Hechos 2:2: «Y de repente vino un estruendo del cielo como de un viento recio que soplaba, el cual llenó toda la casa donde estaban sentados». La palabra griega para «viento» aquí es en realidad pnoê, un primo cercano de pneuma (misma raíz, diferente terminación). Dos versículos más adelante el Pneuma Santo llena a los discípulos. Hechos 2 deliberadamente corre el juego de palabras viento-y-Espíritu a través de un solo párrafo. Los discípulos primero oyen el viento, luego reciben el Espíritu, y hablan en lenguas para que visitantes de dieciséis naciones oigan cada uno el evangelio en su propio idioma materno. El primer sonido de la era de la iglesia fue el sonido del pneuma. El primer milagro de la era de la iglesia fue el idioma. (Estás estudiando el curso correcto.)

blocks.en: How this changes Bible reading
blocks.es_reference: Cómo esto cambia la lectura bíblica

blocks.en: When you read "Holy Spirit" in your English New Testament, you are reading Pneuma Hagion. When the wind blows past your face on a quiet evening — that, too, is pneuma. The God who made the wind made you to breathe and made your soul to be filled with His Spirit. Christianity is not a set of moral rules. It is a wind-filled life. You cannot see pneuma. You can only see what He does.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando lees «Espíritu Santo» en tu Nuevo Testamento, estás leyendo Pneuma Hagion. Cuando el viento sopla en tu rostro en una tarde tranquila — eso también es pneuma. El Dios que hizo el viento te hizo para respirar e hizo tu alma para ser llenada con Su Espíritu. El cristianismo no es un conjunto de reglas morales. Es una vida llena de viento. No puedes ver al pneuma. Solo puedes ver lo que hace.

blocks.en: V. The Four Words Together — and the Bridge to Unit 9
blocks.es_reference: V. Las cuatro palabras juntas — y el puente a la Unidad 9

blocks.en: Look back at our scripture, John 1:14, and read it again with new eyes: "And the Word (Logos) became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace (charis) and truth." Two of our four words sit in plain view. The other two stand close by — John 1:13 says we are born "of God" (begetting by the Pneuma, John 3), and 1 John 4:8 declares "God is agapê." The whole Gospel of John, in fact, is an extended meditation on these four words.
blocks.es_reference: Mira atrás a nuestra escritura, Juan 1:14, y léela de nuevo con nuevos ojos: «Y aquel Verbo (Logos) fue hecho carne, y habitó entre nosotros, y vimos su gloria, gloria como del unigénito del Padre, lleno de gracia (charis) y de verdad». Dos de nuestras cuatro palabras están a la vista. Las otras dos están cerca — Juan 1:13 dice que somos nacidos «de Dios» (engendrados por el Pneuma, Juan 3), y 1 Juan 4:8 declara «Dios es agapê». Todo el Evangelio de Juan, de hecho, es una meditación extendida sobre estas cuatro palabras.

blocks.en: Put them in sequence and you have the whole gospel in four nouns:
blocks.es_reference: Ponlas en secuencia y tienes todo el evangelio en cuatro sustantivos:

blocks.en: <th>Greek</th><th>Meaning</th><th>What it gives the reader</th>
blocks.es_reference: <th>Griego</th><th>Significado</th><th>Lo que le da al lector</th>

blocks.en: LogosThe WordThe Person revealed — God becomes flesh in Christ
blocks.es_reference: LogosEl VerboLa Persona revelada — Dios se hace carne en Cristo

blocks.en: AgapêLoveThe motive that sent Him — God so loved the world
blocks.es_reference: AgapêAmorEl motivo que lo envió — tanto amó Dios al mundo

blocks.en: CharisGraceThe gift He brings — salvation by faith, not by works
blocks.es_reference: CharisGraciaEl regalo que trae — salvación por fe, no por obras

blocks.en: PneumaSpiritThe Breath He gives — new birth, indwelling, power
blocks.es_reference: PneumaEspírituEl Aliento que da — nuevo nacimiento, morada, poder

blocks.en: Logos is what God did. Agapê is why He did it. Charis is what we receive. Pneuma is how we live afterward. Four Greek words, the whole story of redemption. The Bible is one Book, one Author, one Theme, one Hero. The four words of Unit 8 unfold that one Hero from four angles.
blocks.es_reference: Logos es lo que Dios hizo. Agapê es por qué lo hizo. Charis es lo que recibimos. Pneuma es cómo vivimos después. Cuatro palabras griegas, toda la historia de la redención. La Biblia es un Libro, un Autor, un Tema, un Héroe. Las cuatro palabras de la Unidad 8 despliegan a ese único Héroe desde cuatro ángulos.

blocks.en: Notebook activity
blocks.es_reference: Actividad de cuaderno

blocks.en: Before you take the examination, do this. Open a notebook to a fresh page. Write the four words across the top: Logos · Agapê · Charis · Pneuma. Under each one, write the English meaning, one verse where it appears, and one sentence describing how this Greek word changes the way you will read that verse from now on. Keep the page. You will refer back to it in Unit 11 when you do your first full word study, and again in your sermon preparation for the rest of your life. Greek does not stay in a textbook. Greek enters your Bible reading and never leaves.
blocks.es_reference: Antes de tomar el examen, haz esto. Abre un cuaderno a una página nueva. Escribe las cuatro palabras al inicio: Logos · Agapê · Charis · Pneuma. Bajo cada una, escribe el significado en español, un versículo donde aparece, y una oración describiendo cómo esta palabra griega cambia la forma en que leerás ese versículo de ahora en adelante. Guarda la página. Te referirás a ella en la Unidad 11 cuando hagas tu primer estudio completo de palabras, y de nuevo en tu preparación de sermones por el resto de tu vida. El griego no se queda en un libro de texto. El griego entra en tu lectura bíblica y no se va.

blocks.en: Where Unit 9 picks up
blocks.es_reference: Donde retoma la Unidad 9

blocks.en: Unit 9 opens four more boxes: pistis (faith), sôzô (save), dikaiosynê (righteousness), and kyrios (Lord). Together with the four words of Unit 8 these eight nouns and verbs form the New Testament's core salvation vocabulary. By the end of Unit 9 you will be able to read Romans 1:16–17 in Greek — the verse that ignited the Reformation when Martin Luther finally understood what Paul meant by the righteousness of God. Then Unit 10 teaches Strong's numbers in your hand, and Unit 11 turns you loose on your first real word study. Two more units. You can see the finish line.
blocks.es_reference: La Unidad 9 abre cuatro cajas más: pistis (fe), sôzô (salvar), dikaiosynê (justicia), y kyrios (Señor). Junto con las cuatro palabras de la Unidad 8 estos ocho sustantivos y verbos forman el vocabulario central de salvación del Nuevo Testamento. Para el final de la Unidad 9 podrás leer Romanos 1:16–17 en griego — el versículo que encendió la Reforma cuando Martín Lutero finalmente entendió lo que Pablo quería decir por la justicia de Dios. Luego la Unidad 10 enseña los números de Strong en tu mano, y la Unidad 11 te suelta en tu primer estudio real de palabras. Dos unidades más. Puedes ver la meta.

mc.stem: In the KJV translation of 1 Corinthians 13, 'faith, hope, charity,' what Greek word stands behind the English 'charity'?
options: Eros
Agapê
Philia
Storgê
mc.why: The Greek word is agapê. Jerome rendered it into Latin as caritas around AD 400; caritas came into English as 'charity' and was used by the KJV translators in 1611. The English word has since narrowed to mean financial donation, but the Greek agapê never narrowed. This is exactly why we learn the Greek word itself.

mc.stem: How did pre-Christian Greek philosophers (like Heraclitus around 500 BC) use the word logos?
options: As the personal name of a Greek god in the Olympian pantheon
To mean a written letter or a postal message
As a Hebrew loan-word meaning 'covenant'
To mean cosmic Reason, principle, or the rational structure holding the universe together
mc.why: Heraclitus of Ephesus and later the Stoics used logos to mean the abstract cosmic Principle behind all reality — the deep impersonal Reason that ordered the universe. When John 1:1 says 'In the beginning was the Logos,' every educated Greek reader recognized the term immediately. John then turned their abstract principle into a Person: Jesus Christ, the eternal Logos who became flesh.

mc.stem: What is John doing with the Greek word logos when he opens his Gospel in John 1:1?
options: Identifying the eternal Logos as a Person — Jesus Christ, who became flesh in John 1:14
Borrowing the term to argue for an abstract impersonal principle behind reality
Translating it directly from the Hebrew word dabar with no change in meaning
Inventing a brand-new Greek word never used before in the Greek-speaking world
mc.why: John takes a familiar Greek philosophical term and detonates it. The educated Greek reader expected an abstract cosmic principle. John says: yes, the Logos exists; and the Logos was with God; and the Logos was God; and the Logos became flesh. The cosmic Principle is a Person, and His name is Jesus. The Greek word logos in John's hands carries the full doctrine of the Incarnation.

mc.stem: How many Greek words for 'love' are there, of the sort C.S. Lewis described in his book The Four Loves?
options: Two — agapê and eros only
Six, as listed in the Septuagint translation of the Old Testament
Four — eros, philia, storgê, agapê
One — agapê is the only Greek word for love
mc.why: Greek has four words where English has one: eros (romantic desire), philia (friendship), storgê (family affection), and agapê (self-giving sacrificial love). C.S. Lewis's 1960 book The Four Loves explains each. The New Testament chose agapê almost exclusively when it spoke of God's love, because the other three were already loaded with meanings that did not fit divine love.

mc.stem: In Greek, what kind of love does the word eros name?
options: Self-giving sacrificial love that seeks the other's good regardless of return
Romantic, passionate, desire-based love — the love of husband and wife in the Song of Solomon
Friendship love — the bond between equals such as David and Jonathan
Family affection — a parent's love for a child
mc.why: Eros is the Greek word for romantic, desire-based love — passionate, urgent, sometimes destructive. The English 'erotic' preserves the root. Eros is not bad in itself (Song of Solomon celebrates it within marriage), but the New Testament avoided eros for divine love because eros is desire-driven and conditional. God's love is not driven by desire for the worthiness of the beloved.

mc.stem: What kind of love is philia in Greek?
options: Friendship — companion-love between equals who share something in common
Romantic desire
Family blood-bond between parent and child
Sacrificial love for an enemy
mc.why: Philia is friendship, the companion-love between people who share something — a craft, a campaign, a faith, a memory. Aristotle wrote whole books on philia. The English 'Philadelphia' means 'brotherly love' (philia + adelphos = brother). David and Jonathan in 1 Samuel 18 is the great biblical example. Philia requires mutual liking; it is conditional in that sense.

mc.stem: What kind of love is storgê in Greek?
options: A form of romantic eros restricted to married couples
The friendship love of co-workers in ministry
A philosophical love of wisdom (philo-sophia)
Family affection — the bond of parent and child, sibling and sibling
mc.why: Storgê is family affection — the love of a mother for her newborn, of siblings raised in the same house, of a grandfather for his grandchild. It is built on blood-relation and shared upbringing. The New Testament uses storgê rarely (Romans 12:10 commands brotherly affection); for divine love it reaches instead for agapê, because God's love is not limited to the family of blood.

mc.stem: Why did the New Testament writers prefer the word agapê over the other three Greek words for love?
options: Because agapê was the most common everyday word for love in classical Greek
Because the Apostle Paul invented the word agapê himself in the 50s AD
Because in classical Greek agapê was a rare, pale, almost empty word — uncontaminated by sexual, friendship, or family meanings — so they could fill it with new theological content
Because agapê was the only Greek word Jesus knew
mc.why: Eros, philia, and storgê were all strong words already — loaded with meanings of desire, mutual friendship, or blood-bond. None of those could carry a love that crosses every tribe, gives without return, and seeks the good of an enemy. Agapê was the colorless near-empty cup of the four. The New Testament writers picked it up and filled it with the very nature of God. By the end of the New Testament, agapê had become the highest word in the Greek language.

mc.stem: In 1 John 4:8 the Greek says 'ho theos agapê estin' (literally 'God love is'). Which English translation captures this most exactly?
options: 'God has love' — meaning love is something God possesses
'God is love' — meaning love is the eternal essence of God's being
'God feels love' — meaning love is one of God's emotions
'God commands love' — meaning love is something God orders us to do
mc.why: The Greek verb 'estin' is the verb 'to be.' God does not merely have agapê; God is agapê. Agapê is the eternal essence of His being — what He has been from before the foundation of the world, when the three Persons of the Trinity poured agapê into one another in unbroken fellowship. He commands us to love because love is what He is.

mc.stem: The Greek word charis (grace) gives English which family of related words?
options: Chord, chorus, choir — all from a musical root
Chart, charter, charm — all from a paper-document root
Charity, charisma, Eucharist (eu-charis-tia = 'good-grace' = thanksgiving)
Charge, character, charcoal — all from a fire-and-mark root
mc.why: The charis family in English is wide: charity (Latin caritas, from agapê but related), charisma (a Spirit-gift), charismatic, Eucharist (literally 'good-grace,' our word for Communion and thanksgiving), and through Latin gratia we also get 'grateful' and 'gratis.' Whenever you hear an English word with 'char' or 'grat' in it that relates to gift or thanks, the Greek charis stands behind.

mc.stem: In classical pre-Christian Greek, what did charis (grace) originally mean?
options: A favor done that placed the receiver under obligation to repay the giver
A completely free gift with no strings or repayment expected, exactly as Paul uses it
A legal contract signed between two parties of equal status
A religious tax paid to the temple of Apollo at Delphi
mc.why: In classical Athens, charis was the favor of a patron that always created obligation. The receiver was bound to repay the giver for life. Paul's Ephesians 2:8–9 deliberately inverts this: God's charis is the kind of favor that creates NO obligation, the kind that excludes boasting precisely because it cannot be repaid. The pagan reader of Paul's letter would have stared at the page — this is not how charis is supposed to work. Exactly. That is the gospel.

mc.stem: How did the New Testament transform the Greek word charis (grace)?
options: By teaching that grace must be earned through good works and sacraments
By restricting grace only to ethnic Israel and excluding the Gentile nations
By replacing the need for faith with the need for ritual purity
By inverting it: grace becomes a FREE gift placing no obligation of repayment on the receiver — pure, unilateral favor from God
mc.why: Paul takes the word that always meant 'favor with obligation' and uses it for the favor that has no obligation. 'By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.' Boasting is impossible in front of a gift this large. The Greek word charis carries the entire Reformation doctrine of salvation by grace alone.

mc.stem: Who wrote the hymn 'Amazing Grace,' and what was his background?
options: Charles Wesley, a Methodist preacher who never went to sea
Isaac Watts, a London hymn-writer of the early 1700s
John Newton, a former slave-ship captain converted in a storm at sea in 1748, who later became an Anglican parson at Olney
Fanny Crosby, the blind American hymn-writer of the late 1800s
mc.why: John Newton (1725–1807) was captain of a slave ship out of Liverpool in his twenties. On March 21, 1748, his ship hit a storm so violent off Ireland that he expected to drown; he cried out to the Christ he had been blaspheming. He survived. He left the slave trade, was ordained Anglican parson at Olney in 1764, and wrote 'Amazing Grace' for his New Year's Day sermon in 1772. His tombstone, written by his own hand, calls him 'once an infidel and libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was by the rich mercy of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long laboured to destroy.'

mc.stem: What does Ephesians 2:8–9 teach about how we are saved?
options: By keeping the Ten Commandments perfectly without failure
By grace (charis) through faith — not of works, so that no one may boast
By a combination of faith and the merit of good works added together
By baptism and faithful church membership
mc.why: Ephesians 2:8–9: 'By grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast.' The Greek charis here is the unrepayable gift — the kind of favor that excludes boasting by definition. Salvation is from start to finish a gift, received by faith, given by God's grace alone. This verse summarized in one Greek word: charis.

mc.stem: What is the range of meanings carried by the single Greek word pneuma?
options: Spirit, wind, and breath — all three carried by one Greek word
Only 'spirit' — never 'wind' or 'breath'
Only 'wind' — 'spirit' is a Christian invention not in classical Greek
Only 'fire' and 'tongue' — from the Pentecost imagery
mc.why: Greek pneuma holds three meanings together: wind (what moves the branches), breath (what fills the lungs), and spirit (what indwells the soul). English splits them into three words; Greek keeps them as one Reality with three windows. Hebrew did the very same thing with ruach in the Old Testament. The biblical mind refuses to separate the moving invisible breath of the wind from the moving invisible breath of the Spirit of God.

mc.stem: Which English medical word comes directly from the Greek pneuma?
options: Cardiology — the study of the heart
Dermatitis — inflammation of the skin
Hemoglobin — the iron-protein in red blood cells
Pneumonia — a disease of the lungs (the organ where breath happens)
mc.why: Pneumonia, pneumatic, pneumatic tire, pneumatic drill — the 'pneum' family of English words preserves the Greek pneuma. The English word 'spirit' itself comes from Latin spiritus ('breath'), preserving the same idea at a second remove. Wherever you see 'pneum' in an English or Spanish word, the Greek pneuma stands behind it.

mc.stem: In John 3:8 Jesus tells Nicodemus, 'The wind blows where it wishes … so is everyone born of the Spirit.' What is the Greek wordplay that the English translation cannot fully capture?
options: Greek uses the same word (pneuma) for both 'wind' and 'Spirit' — Jesus is making a single pun the English splits into two words
There is no wordplay — wind and Spirit are completely unrelated words in Greek
The verse was added to John's Gospel by later scribes and is not original
Jesus is correcting Nicodemus's pronunciation of a Hebrew word
mc.why: Both 'wind' and 'Spirit' in John 3:8 are the same Greek word, pneuma. Jesus deliberately holds them together: 'the pneuma blows where it wills … so is everyone born of the pneuma.' You cannot see this thing, but you can see what it does. The leaves move — you know there is wind. The sinner is reborn — you know there is Spirit. Same invisible Reality, two domains. The English splits the word; the Greek hearer would catch the pun instantly.

mc.stem: What does Acts 2:2 describe as the sound of Pentecost morning when the Holy Spirit fell upon the disciples?
options: A sound from heaven like a rushing mighty wind that filled the whole house
A still small voice like the one Elijah heard at Horeb
Total silence for one full hour
A trumpet blast from Mount Zion announcing the new covenant
mc.why: Acts 2:2 reports a sound from heaven 'as of a rushing mighty wind' filling the upper room. The Greek word for 'wind' here is pnoê, a close cousin of pneuma (same root). Two verses later the Holy Pneuma fills the disciples. Acts 2 deliberately runs the wind-and-Spirit wordplay across a single paragraph. The first sound of the church age was the sound of pneuma, and the first miracle of the church age was language. (You are studying the right course.)

mc.stem: Our unit scripture, John 1:14 ('And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us … full of grace and truth'), contains TWO of our four key Greek words from this unit. Which two?
options: Agapê and pneuma
Eros and storgê
Logos and charis (Word and grace)
Pneuma and agapê
mc.why: John 1:14 contains 'Logos' ('the Word became flesh') and 'charis' ('full of grace and truth'). John could not have introduced the doctrine of the Incarnation more economically: the eternal Logos taking on flesh, and the gift He brings is charis. Two words. The whole Christmas story.

mc.stem: The four Greek words of Unit 8 unfold the gospel in this order. Fill in the blanks: Logos = the ____; Agapê = the love that ____; Charis = the gift He ____; Pneuma = the breath He ____.
options: Sermon revealed / saves Him / counts / takes back
Principle revealed / surrounds Him / earns / sells
Place revealed / loses Him / withholds / hides
Person revealed (Christ) / sent Him / brings / gives (new birth)
mc.why: Logos is what God did (the Person revealed). Agapê is why He did it (the love that sent Him). Charis is what we receive (the gift He brings). Pneuma is how we live afterward (the breath He gives). Four Greek words, the whole story of redemption. The Bible is one Book, one Author, one Theme, one Hero. The four words of Unit 8 show that one Hero from four angles.
